set.body:
TESTED THE MOST DANGEROUS THING ABOUT A LEARNED METRIC and the package handles it correctly. If the noise metric were trained on the same partitions being compared, crossnobis distances would be circular and biased away from zero. They are not.

THE DEFAULT IS THE SAFE POLICY, and it is declared rather than implied:

  formals(plan_crossnobis)$training
    -> metric_training_policy("exclude_evaluation")

  metric_training_policy()
    kind                            exclude_evaluation
    includes_evaluation_residuals   FALSE
    assumption                      partition_disjoint_metric_training
    signature                       sha256:c24cdf453e7f2c48b0cc41f662c41662d29f4d85...

So the object carries a named policy, an explicit assumption string, and a content signature. This is the package's declare-everything discipline applied to exactly the place where it matters most statistically.

EMPIRICAL CONFIRMATION. 120 null replicates, 24 features, 4 runs, 3 conditions, 60 timepoints, searchlight frame, shrinkage metric:

  mean crossnobis  +0.00103   se 0.00089   z = +1.17   unbiased

Leakage would show up as a positive bias - a metric fitted to the evaluation residuals shrinks exactly the noise directions present in those residuals, inflating the apparent distance. There is no such bias.

I AM CORRECTING MY OWN EARLIER CRITICISM. On bd-01KZY9FGVJ0JXCB1Q1KN88AE6D and in messages to claude-review I flagged that plan_crossnobis defaults metric = shrinkage_precision(), called it 'a silent statistical choice made for the user', and argued it sits badly beside the package forcing  to be explicit. That framing was too broad and I want it narrowed on the evidence.

  WHAT STANDS   the shrinkage INTENSITY is chosen for the user without comment, and a
                shrinkage intensity does affect the resulting distances.
  WHAT I GOT WRONG  I implied metric learning generally is handled loosely here. The
                opposite is true. The genuinely hazardous dimension of metric learning -
                whether the metric sees the data it will be used to evaluate - is handled
                with MORE explicitness than almost anything else in the package: a named
                policy object, a written assumption, and a signature.

So the criticism narrows from 'the metric defaults are inconsistent with the package's stance' to 'the shrinkage intensity is the one metric parameter chosen silently, while everything around it is declared'. That is a much smaller point and arguably not worth changing - a default intensity with a documented value may be the right call, where a default train/test policy would not be.

DOCUMENTATION CONSEQUENCE, which is the actionable part. metric_training_policy is on the list of exports appearing in no vignette (bd-01KZYARD5697TRN2Q3S0E153BM). A reader evaluating whether to trust this package's crossnobis numbers against rsatoolbox or PCM would want to know that train/test separation is enforced and declared. They cannot currently find that out, which is the same undersold-capability pattern as bd-01KZYR0Y29S6G7FVY2VP61QZFW - the fourth instance.
set.title: Verified: learned-metric training is leakage-free by default, and the policy is explicitly declared
